questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Tangent
questions.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $16{x}^{2}=(4x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+16{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+(4x)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(4x)}{4}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{3|x|\sqrt{9{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|3x|\sqrt{(3x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $3x.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3|x|\sqrt{9{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|3x|\sqrt{(3x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\frac{\text{arcsec}(3x)}{3}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Tangent
questions.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8}{16+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{8}{16\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/16)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/16}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{4}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8}{16+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (4\,\text{d}u) \\  & =2\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =2\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{4})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{5}{|x|\sqrt{100{x}^{2}-1}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{50}{|10x|\sqrt{(10x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $10x.$

So, let's substitute $u=10x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=10\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{10}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{|x|\sqrt{100{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{50}{|10x|\sqrt{(10x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =50\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{10}\text{d}u) \\  & =50\cdot \frac{1}{10}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =5\,\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =5\,\text{arcsec}(10x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{3+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{3\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/3)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+(x/\sqrt{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{3+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+(x/\sqrt{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}/3}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}/3}\frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{3}/3} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot \frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{9}\end{aligned}
$$
